title: 13  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 13.9 The result that should bother you
text:
13.9 The result that should bother you
The line’s in-sample mean squared error is 847.5. The mean squared error of ignoring age entirely and predicting 119.9 for everyone is 863.2. Fitting removed 1.8% of the squared error.
Now destroy the relationship on purpose and fit again. Shuffling the age column breaks any link between a patient’s age and their glucose while leaving both distributions exactly as they were.

RPython



set.seed(42)
glu_shuffled <- glu |> mutate(age = sample(age))

fit_shuffled  <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu_shuffled)
pred_shuffled <- predict(fit_shuffled, new_data = glu_shuffled)$.pred

coef(extract_fit_engine(fit_shuffled))

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 128.7674274  -0.2665893

mean((glu_shuffled$glucose - pred_shuffled)^2)

#> [1] 849.8275





rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
glu_shuffled = glu.assign(age=rng.permutation(glu["age"].values))

fit_shuffled = LinearRegression().fit(glu_shuffled[["age"]], glu_shuffled["glucose"])
mse_shuffled = np.mean((glu_shuffled["glucose"]
                        - fit_shuffled.predict(glu_shuffled[["age"]]))**2)

fit_shuffled.intercept_, fit_shuffled.coef_[0], mse_shuffled

#> (np.float64(116.54068704973496), np.float64(0.10099400075956573), np.float64(861.2722501680768))





Three steps of reasoning.

Shuffled age cannot predict glucose. Any apparent fit is coincidence, and its error is what “no relationship at all” looks like in these units.
The shuffled fit’s error is around 850 in R and around 861 in Python — the two seeds shuffle differently — against 847.5 for the real age column and 863.2 for the baseline. The real predictor buys you almost nothing that a deliberately broken one does not.
The algebra in Chapter 16 is exact, the fit is genuinely the best straight line there is, and the model is still not worth deploying. A minimum is not the same thing as a small number.

Keep this: the entire day is about finding the best line, and the best line here is nearly useless. Being able to hold both of those at once is the point.

title: 13  Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning
section: 13.10 Task 3 — Change the algorithm, keep everything else
text:
13.10 Task 3 — Change the algorithm, keep everything else
A decision tree is a different learning algorithm applied to the identical dataset and the identical question. You meet trees properly in Chapter 26; for now, swap one line and look at the shape of what comes out.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

dt_model <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("______")
dt_fit   <- dt_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

rpart.plot(extract_fit_engine(dt_fit), roundint = FALSE)







TipStuck?





The engine is the package that does the work, exactly as "lm" was for linear_reg(). For trees in R it is the recursive-partitioning package, and the string is its name.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text

tree_reg = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(______, ______)
print(export_text(tree_reg, feature_names=["age"]))







TipStuck?





The tree takes the same two arguments the linear model took, in the same order.






Now plot both models’ predictions over the data. The line is a line; the tree is a staircase, constant within each age band it chose.

RPython



dt_fit_shown <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("rpart") |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

glu_pred <- glu |>
  mutate(pred_tree = predict(dt_fit_shown, new_data = glu)$.pred,
         pred_line = predict(ls_fit,       new_data = glu)$.pred)

ggplot(glu_pred, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = glucose), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_step(aes(y = pred_tree), colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred_line), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)")











from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
tree_shown = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(X, y)

grid = pd.DataFrame({"age": np.linspace(glu["age"].min(), glu["age"].max(), 400)})
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.5)
ax.plot(grid["age"], tree_shown.predict(grid), color="darkred")
ax.plot(grid["age"], lin_reg.predict(grid), color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)"); ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
plt.show()











The tree’s in-sample mean squared error is lower than the line’s: 685.7 in R with rpart’s default pruning, 677.9 in Python with a depth of 3. Both are well below the line’s 847.5. The tree is not better. It has more parameters — one mean per leaf rather than two numbers for the whole dataset — and more parameters always fit the rows you fitted them to more closely. Chapter 26 is where that argument gets settled.






NoteThe two trees are not the same tree



rpart and scikit-learn choose splits the same way but stop differently: rpart prunes using a complexity parameter and cross-validation, scikit-learn stops when you tell it to. Ours end up with six leaves and seven respectively. Unlike the linear coefficients, which agreed to the decimal, the trees are a genuine difference between the two libraries’ defaults, and you should expect to have to state tree-stopping rules explicitly whenever you report one.

13.14 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can fit, read and apply a two-parameter model in both languages, swap the learning algorithm without touching anything else, and state what the dataset contributed to the result.
Cannot: that this line is the best one. We never defined “best” — we used whatever lm() optimises, which happens to be squared error. That choice does real work, and it is Chapter 14.

14.2 Why this, here
Chapter 13 fitted a line and called it the best fit, without ever saying best at what. This exercise supplies the missing definition. A loss function scores a candidate line against the data; the fitting procedure returns the line with the lowest score. Change the score and you change the line — and then Chapter 15 asks how the lowest score is found at all.

title: 14  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 14.5 Four ways to add up 80 mistakes
text:
14.5 Four ways to add up 80 mistakes
Residuals are positive and negative, so adding them cancels most of the error away. Two repairs are in common use, and they are not equivalent.
\[\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \left| r_i \right|\]
Squaring is the L2 loss; taking the absolute value is the L1 loss. The mean squared error is the sum of squared residuals divided by the number of rows, so it does not grow simply because the dataset is larger. The root of the MSE — RMSE — is back in the outcome’s units and is easier to quote.

RPython



loss_table <- function(residuals) {
  m <- length(residuals)              # the number of residuals passed in,
  ssr <- sum(residuals^2)             # not the size of some data frame
  c(SSR = ssr, MSE = ssr / m, RMSE = sqrt(ssr / m),
    MAE = mean(abs(residuals)))
}

round(loss_table(glu$resid_guess), 3)

#>       SSR       MSE      RMSE       MAE 
#> 90868.250  1135.853    33.702    28.656





def loss_table(residuals):
    residuals = np.asarray(residuals)
    m = len(residuals)
    ssr = np.sum(residuals**2)
    return {"SSR": ssr, "MSE": ssr / m, "RMSE": np.sqrt(ssr / m),
            "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(residuals))}

{k: round(v, 3) for k, v in loss_table(glu["resid_guess"]).items()}

#> {'SSR': np.float64(90868.25), 'MSE': np.float64(1135.853), 'RMSE': np.float64(33.702), 'MAE': np.float64(28.656)}





The hand-drawn line scores SSR 90868, MSE 1135.9, RMSE 33.7 and MAE 28.7. RMSE and MAE are both in mg/dL and the RMSE is the larger of the two, which is not an accident: squaring weights the worst patients more heavily, so any summary built from squares sits above the plain average error whenever the residuals are unequal.

Three glucose values are recorded three times too large — a plausible unit or transcription error. Multiply rows 1, 3 and 5 by three, refit, and compare.

title: 14  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 14.8 The result that should bother you
text:
14.8 The result that should bother you
The obvious reading is that outliers break regression. They do not. They break this loss.
Fit the same straight line by minimising mean absolute error instead of mean squared error. There is no closed form, so hand the loss to a general-purpose optimiser.

RPython



fit_lad <- function(data) {
  loss <- function(p) mean(abs(data$glucose - (p[1] + p[2] * data$age)))
  optim(c(mean(data$glucose), 0), loss, method = "Nelder-Mead",
        control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-12))$par
}

glu_bad <- glu
glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] <- glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] * 3

rbind(clean = fit_lad(glu), contaminated = fit_lad(glu_bad))

#>                 [,1]   [,2]
#> clean        101.875 0.4375
#> contaminated 101.875 0.4375





from scipy.optimize import minimize

def fit_lad(data):
    loss = lambda p: np.mean(np.abs(data["glucose"] - (p[0] + p[1] * data["age"])))
    return minimize(loss, [data["glucose"].mean(), 0.0], method="Nelder-Mead",
                    options={"maxiter": 5000, "fatol": 1e-12, "xatol": 1e-10}).x

glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] = glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] * 3

{"clean": fit_lad(glu), "contaminated": fit_lad(glu_bad)}

#> {'clean': array([101.875 ,   0.4375]), 'contaminated': array([101.875 ,   0.4375])}





Three steps of reasoning.

The least-absolute-error line is intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the clean data — and intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the contaminated data. To four decimal places, the contamination did not move it at all. Both languages agree, having started from the same guess and minimised the same function.
Squaring is the mechanism. Tripling a glucose of 194 to 582 multiplies its contribution to the MSE by roughly the square of how far out it now is, so the line is dragged towards it; under absolute error that patient contributes its distance and no more, and three votes out of eighty do not carry.
So “the best fit line” is not a property of the data. It is a property of the data and the loss you chose, and the choice was made for you by whoever wrote lm().







NoteWhy squared error anyway



If absolute error is this much more robust, why is every default squared? Two reasons, and only one of them is about statistics. The squared loss is differentiable everywhere, which is what lets Chapter 15 follow a gradient and Chapter 16 solve for the answer in closed form; absolute error has a kink at zero and needs a different class of algorithm. And the mean is the minimiser of squared error while the median minimises absolute error, so the two losses are answering different questions about the outcome, not the same question with different robustness. Convenience, then interpretation — in that order, historically.

title: 14  Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions
section: 14.9 How the loss changes as the line moves
text:
14.9 How the loss changes as the line moves
So far a loss has scored a line someone else supplied. Now treat it as a function of the parameters, which is what fitting actually optimises:
\[\text{MSE}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}
\left( y_i - \left( \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i \right) \right)^2\]
Start by hand with the first three patients, aged 28, 44 and 26, with glucose 194, 129 and 132. For \(\hat\beta_0 = 3\) and \(\hat\beta_1 = 5\) the predictions are 143, 223 and 133, so
\[\frac{(194-143)^2 + (129-223)^2 + (132-133)^2}{3}
= \frac{2601 + 8836 + 1}{3} = 3812.67\]

fit_ols <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

grid <- expand_grid(b0 = seq(60, 160, by = 1),
                    b1 = seq(-1, 2, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(MSE = map2_dbl(b0, b1, ~ mse_of(.x, .y, glu$age, glu$glucose)))

ggplot(grid, aes(x = b0, y = b1)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = log10(MSE))) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = log10(MSE)), colour = "white", alpha = 0.4, bins = 12) +
  annotate("point", x = coef(fit_ols)[[1]], y = coef(fit_ols)[[2]],
           colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[0]), y = expression(hat(beta)[1]),
       fill = "log10(MSE)")











from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
fit_ols = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"])

def mse_of(beta0, beta1, x, y):
    return np.mean((y - (beta0 + beta1 * x))**2)

b0_vals = np.arange(60, 160.001, 1.0)
b1_vals = np.arange(-1, 2.0001, 0.02)
B0, B1 = np.meshgrid(b0_vals, b1_vals, indexing="ij")
resid_grid = glu["glucose"].values - (B0[..., None] + B1[..., None] * glu["age"].values)
MSE = (resid_grid**2).mean(axis=-1)       # average over patients, not parameters

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cs = ax.contourf(B0, B1, np.log10(MSE), levels=20, cmap="magma")
ax.scatter([fit_ols.intercept_], [fit_ols.coef_[0]], color="red", zorder=3)
fig.colorbar(cs, ax=ax, label="log10(MSE)")

#> <matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar object at 0x17d25cb50>

ax.set_xlabel(r"$\hat\beta_0$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\hat\beta_1$")
plt.show()











Two features of that picture matter for the next exercise. The surface is a bowl: it has one lowest point and no others, which is why least squares has a single answer. And the bowl is a long diagonal trough rather than a round basin, because the intercept and the slope trade off against each other — raise the slope and you can compensate by lowering the intercept. Chapter 15 walks downhill on this exact surface, and the shape of the trough is what makes that harder than it sounds.

title: 15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
text:
15.2 Why this, here
Chapter 14 found the lowest point of a loss surface by evaluating 15,251 candidate lines. That works for two parameters and nothing larger. Every model you will meet after this week — logistic regression on Day 4, and anything with a neural network in it afterwards — is fitted by the method on this page instead: start somewhere, measure which way is downhill, take a step, repeat.

15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent

title: 15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
text:
15.3 The update rule
\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \alpha f'(x_n)\]

\(x_n\) is the current guess.
\(f'(x_n)\) is the derivative of the function at that guess — the slope.
\(\alpha\) is the learning rate: a small positive number controlling step size.

The minus sign carries the whole idea. Where the slope is positive the function rises to the right, so we subtract and move left; where it is negative we subtract a negative and move right. Either way the step is against the slope, and the steeper the slope the bigger the step.

title: 15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
text:
15.4 Minimising \(f(x) = x^2\)
The derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\), so the rule becomes \(x_{n+1} = x_n - 2\alpha
x_n\). We know the answer is \(x = 0\), which is why this is the example: you can see whether the algorithm is working.

RPython



library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(patchwork)

f       <- function(x) x^2
f_prime <- function(x) 2 * x

curve_df <- data.frame(x = seq(-10, 10, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(f_x = f(x), f_prime_x = f_prime(x))

p1 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_x)) + geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = expression(f(x) == x^2), y = "f(x)")
p2 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_prime_x)) + geom_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = expression(paste(f, "'", (x) == 2 * x)), y = "f'(x)")
p1 + p2











import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

f       = lambda x: x**2
f_prime = lambda x: 2 * x

xs = np.linspace(-10, 10, 200)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
axes[0].plot(xs, f(xs), color="steelblue");  axes[0].set_title("f(x) = x^2")
axes[1].plot(xs, f_prime(xs), color="firebrick"); axes[1].set_title("f'(x) = 2x")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()











Start at \(x = -10\) with \(\alpha = 0.8\) and take ten steps.

The guess goes −10, 6, −3.6, 2.16, −1.296 and so on: it crosses the minimum every single step and lands closer each time. Overshooting is not failure. With \(\alpha = 0.8\) each step is 1.6 times the distance to the minimum, so the sign flips and the magnitude shrinks by 0.6.

RPython



steps_df <- data.frame(step = 1:10, x = path) |> mutate(f_x = f(x))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_x)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +

             shape = 21, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "yellow", high = "red") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)", fill = "step")











fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(xs, f(xs), color="grey")
sc = ax.scatter(path, [f(v) for v in path], c=range(1, len(path) + 1),
                cmap="autumn_r", edgecolor="black", zorder=3)

15.5 Task 1 — Your turn, on a function whose minimum you can check
Minimise
\[f(x) = x^2 + 3x + 5\]
Differentiate it on paper first: you should get \(f'(x) = 2x + 3\), which is zero at \(x = -1.5\). Then write the loop and see whether the algorithm agrees with your algebra.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

g       <- function(x) x^2 + 3 * x + 5
g_prime <- function(x) ______

alpha <- 0.1
x     <- 2
for (i in 1:40) {
  x <- x - ______ * g_prime(x)
}
check_matches(x, -1.5, label = "minimiser of x^2 + 3x + 5")







TipStuck?





The derivative of \(ax^2\) is \(2ax\), the derivative of \(bx\) is \(b\), and the derivative of a constant is zero. The second blank is the step size, which is already defined above the loop.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

g       = lambda x: x**2 + 3 * x + 5
g_prime = lambda x: ______

alpha = 0.1
x = 2.0
for i in range(40):
    x = x - ______ * g_prime(x)

check_matches(x, -1.5, label="minimiser of x^2 + 3x + 5")




Forty steps get you to −1.4995. The algorithm approaches the minimum and never arrives, which is true of gradient descent in general: you stop when the improvement stops mattering, not when the gradient is zero.

section: 15.6 The learning rate is the whole game
text:
15.6 The learning rate is the whole game
Run the same problem — \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x = -10\) — at four learning rates for twenty steps each.

RPython



descend_1d <- function(alpha, x0 = -10, n = 20) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- x - alpha * f_prime(x)
  x
}

rates <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.8, 1.0, 1.05)
data.frame(alpha = rates,
           final_x = sapply(rates, descend_1d),
           final_f = sapply(rates, function(a) f(descend_1d(a))))

#>   alpha       final_x      final_f
#> 1  0.01 -6.676080e+00 4.457004e+01
#> 2  0.10 -1.152922e-01 1.329228e-02
#> 3  0.80 -3.656158e-04 1.336749e-07
#> 4  1.00 -1.000000e+01 1.000000e+02
#> 5  1.05 -6.727500e+01 4.525926e+03





import pandas as pd

def descend_1d(alpha, x0=-10.0, n=20):
    x = x0
    for _ in range(n):
        x = x - alpha * f_prime(x)
    return x

rates = [0.01, 0.1, 0.8, 1.0, 1.05]
pd.DataFrame({"alpha": rates,
              "final_x": [descend_1d(a) for a in rates],
              "final_f": [f(descend_1d(a)) for a in rates]})

#>    alpha    final_x       final_f
#> 0   0.01  -6.676080  4.457004e+01
#> 1   0.10  -0.115292  1.329228e-02
#> 2   0.80  -0.000366  1.336749e-07
#> 3   1.00 -10.000000  1.000000e+02
#> 4   1.05 -67.274999  4.525926e+03





Read that table carefully, because every row is a different lesson.








\(\alpha\)
After 20 steps
What happened




0.01
\(x = -6.68\)
correct direction, far too slow — it needs thousands of steps


0.1
\(x = -0.115\)
steady approach from one side


0.8
\(x = -0.00037\)
overshoots every step and converges fastest of the five


1.0
\(x = -10\)
bounces between −10 and 10 for ever, making no progress at all


1.05
\(x = -67.3\)
diverges: each step is further out than the last



The fastest rate here is not the smallest one, and the boundary between working and diverging is sharp. For \(f(x)=x^2\) the step multiplies the distance to the minimum by \((1 - 2\alpha)\), so anything below 1 converges, 1 exactly cycles, and above 1 explodes. There is no warning and no error message: at \(\alpha = 1.05\) the loop runs happily and returns a number.






WarningA run that finished is not a run that worked



Nothing in any of those five runs raised an error. If you only look at the final number, the diverging run and the converging run are indistinguishable in form — both are a number. Always print the path, or the loss, and look at whether it is going down.

title: 15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
text:
15.8 Local and global minima
Everything above had one minimum. Now take
\[f(x) = x^4 + x^3 - 2x^2 \qquad f'(x) = 4x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x\]
which has two: a shallow one near \(x = 0.69\) and a deeper one near \(x = -1.44\).

RPython



h       <- function(x) x^4 + x^3 - 2 * x^2
h_prime <- function(x) 4 * x^3 + 3 * x^2 - 4 * x

descend_h <- function(x0, alpha = 0.03, n = 200) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- x - alpha * h_prime(x)
  c(start = x0, end = x, f_end = h(x))
}

t(sapply(c(1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2), descend_h))

#>      start        end      f_end
#> [1,]   1.0  0.6930005 -0.3970463
#> [2,]   0.2  0.6930005 -0.3970463
#> [3,]   0.0  0.0000000  0.0000000
#> [4,]  -0.1 -1.4430005 -2.8334224
#> [5,]  -0.5 -1.4430005 -2.8334224
#> [6,]   2.0  0.6930005 -0.3970463





h       = lambda x: x**4 + x**3 - 2 * x**2
h_prime = lambda x: 4 * x**3 + 3 * x**2 - 4 * x

def descend_h(x0, alpha=0.03, n=200):
    x = float(x0)
    for _ in range(n):
        x = x - alpha * h_prime(x)
    return {"start": x0, "end": x, "f_end": h(x)}

pd.DataFrame([descend_h(s) for s in (1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)])

#>    start    end     f_end
#> 0    1.0  0.693 -0.397046
#> 1    0.2  0.693 -0.397046
#> 2    0.0  0.000  0.000000
#> 3   -0.1 -1.443 -2.833422
#> 4   -0.5 -1.443 -2.833422
#> 5    2.0  0.693 -0.397046






RPython



curve_h <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 1.5, length.out = 300)) |> mutate(f_x = h(x))
ends    <- data.frame(start = c(1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)) |>
  mutate(end = sapply(start, function(s) descend_h(s)[["end"]]), f_end = h(end))

ggplot(curve_h, aes(x, f_x)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = ends, aes(x = end, y = f_end), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)")











grid_h = np.linspace(-2, 1.5, 300)
ends = [descend_h(s)["end"] for s in (1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(grid_h, h(grid_h), color="grey")
ax.scatter(ends, [h(e) for e in ends], color="red", zorder=3)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("f(x)")
plt.show()











Starting at 1, 0.2 or 2 lands on \(x = 0.693\), where \(f = -0.397\). Starting at −0.1 or −0.5 lands on \(x = -1.443\), where \(f = -2.833\) — seven times lower. Nothing distinguishes the two runs except where they began, and neither run can tell you it stopped in the worse of the two places.
Starting at exactly 0 is the strangest case: the derivative there is zero, so the first step moves nowhere and every step after it moves nowhere. Gradient descent stops at any stationary point, and \(x = 0\) here is a local maximum.






NoteWhy this does not ruin least squares



The MSE surface you plotted in Chapter 14 is a bowl with one minimum — convex, in the technical term — so for linear regression this whole worry is moot: every starting point reaches the same answer. The worry is real for almost everything else, which is why deep learning papers report random seeds, and why “we trained it twice and got different models” is a sentence you will hear.

text:
15.10 Two parameters at once
A loss has as many derivatives as it has parameters. Collect them into a gradient vector and the update rule is unchanged — it just applies to every parameter simultaneously. For
\[f(x, y) = x\sin(y) + x^2 \qquad
\nabla f = \left\langle \sin(y) + 2x,\; x\cos(y) \right\rangle\]

RPython



fxy <- function(x, y) x * sin(y) + x^2
grad_x <- function(x, y) sin(y) + 2 * x
grad_y <- function(x, y) x * cos(y)

x <- 1; y <- 2; alpha <- 0.01
trace_xy <- data.frame(iter = 0, x = x, y = y, f = fxy(x, y))

for (i in 1:1000) {
  gx <- grad_x(x, y); gy <- grad_y(x, y)
  x <- x - alpha * gx
  y <- y - alpha * gy
  if (i %% 100 == 0)
    trace_xy <- rbind(trace_xy, data.frame(iter = i, x = x, y = y, f = fxy(x, y)))
}
trace_xy

#>    iter          x        y          f
#> 1     0  1.0000000 2.000000  1.9092974
#> 2   100 -0.2426550 2.084195 -0.1524906
#> 3   200 -0.4284631 1.933253 -0.2170447

grad_y = lambda x, y: x * np.cos(y)

x, y, alpha = 1.0, 2.0, 0.01
rows = [{"iter": 0, "x": x, "y": y, "f": fxy(x, y)}]

for i in range(1, 1001):
    gx, gy = grad_x(x, y), grad_y(x, y)
    x, y = x - alpha * gx, y - alpha * gy
    if i % 100 == 0:
        rows.append({"iter": i, "x": x, "y": y, "f": fxy(x, y)})

pd.DataFrame(rows)

#>     iter         x         y         f
#> 0      0  1.000000  2.000000  1.909297
#> 1    100 -0.242655  2.084195 -0.152491
#> 2    200 -0.428463  1.933253 -0.217045
#> 3    300 -0.474188  1.801955 -0.236721
#> 4    400 -0.490187  1.713580 -0.244915
#> 5    500 -0.496295  1.657935 -0.248103
#> 6    600 -0.498618  1.623729 -0.249300
#> 7    700 -0.499489  1.602895 -0.249742
#> 8    800 -0.499812  1.590248 -0.249905
#> 9    900 -0.499931  1.582581 -0.249965
#> 10  1000 -0.499975  1.577936 -0.249987





It reaches \(x = -0.5\), \(y = 1.578\), \(f = -0.25\), which is the exact minimum of this function: for any \(y\) the best \(x\) is \(-\sin(y)/2\), giving \(f = -\sin^2(y)/4\), smallest when \(\sin y = 1\). Notice how much of the progress happens early — after 100 iterations \(f\) is already −0.153, and the remaining 900 buy −0.097.






NotePartial derivatives by hand, and when not to



We differentiated \(f\) twice by hand, once per variable. For a model with a million parameters nobody does that: the derivatives are generated mechanically — symbolically, as a computer algebra system would, or by automatic differentiation, which is what every deep learning framework is at bottom. Knowing that the gradient is just a list of slopes is enough to read those tools’ output.

title: 15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 15.11 The result that should bother you
text:
15.11 The result that should bother you
Now put the method on the actual problem: find the intercept and slope that minimise the MSE for glucose against age, by gradient descent instead of by lm(). The gradients of \(\text{MSE}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \frac{1}{m}\sum (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\) are
\[\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_0} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum r_i
\qquad
\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_1} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum x_i r_i\]
with \(r_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\). Chapter 16 derives them.

RPython



library(readr)
diab <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu  <- diab |> filter(glucose > 0) |> slice(1:80) |> select(age, glucose)

descend_mse <- function(x, y, alpha, n) {
  b0 <- 0; b1 <- 0
  mse <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    r  <- y - (b0 + b1 * x)
    b0 <- b0 - alpha * (-2 * mean(r))
    b1 <- b1 - alpha * (-2 * mean(x * r))
    mse[i] <- mean((y - (b0 + b1 * x))^2)
  }
  list(b0 = b0, b1 = b1, mse = mse)
}

raw <- descend_mse(glu$age, glu$glucose, alpha = 1e-4, n = 1000)
c(intercept = raw$b0, slope = raw$b1, MSE = tail(raw$mse, 1))

#>   intercept       slope         MSE 
#>    3.234060    3.040203 2512.521591

coef(lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu))

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 110.2979509   0.2886749





import pandas as pd
diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80).reset_index(drop=True))

def descend_mse(x, y, alpha, n):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    b0 = b1 = 0.0
    mse = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        r = y - (b0 + b1 * x)
        b0 = b0 - alpha * (-2 * r.mean())
        b1 = b1 - alpha * (-2 * (x * r).mean())
        mse[i] = np.mean((y - (b0 + b1 * x))**2)
    return {"b0": b0, "b1": b1, "mse": mse}

raw = descend_mse(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=1e-4, n=1000)
raw["b0"], raw["b1"], raw["mse"][-1]

#> (np.float64(3.2340597363518033), np.float64(3.040202790594225), np.float64(2512.5215912023486))





After a thousand iterations the descent reports an intercept of 3.23 and a slope of 3.04, with an MSE of 2513. The correct answer is 110.298 and 0.2887, with an MSE of 847.5. The descent is not close, and it is worse than predicting the mean glucose for everybody, which scores 863.
Three steps of reasoning.

The run did not fail. The MSE went down at every iteration and the loop finished without complaint. Had we only printed the final parameters and drawn a line through the data, the plot would have looked plausible.
The cause is the shape of the surface from Chapter 14: a long diagonal trough, not a round bowl. Age has a mean of 33 and glucose a mean of 120, so the \(\beta_1\) gradient is hundreds of times larger than the \(\beta_0\) one. Any learning rate small enough to keep \(\beta_1\) stable leaves \(\beta_0\) crawling. Raising \(\alpha\) to \(10^{-3}\) does not fix it either — try it, and watch both parameters overflow to infinity within a few hundred steps.
This is the usual failure of gradient descent on raw clinical data: not a wrong answer that announces itself, but a right-shaped answer that is nowhere near the optimum. The published version of this material reported those unconverged numbers as the optimised parameters.

The fix is to standardise both columns — subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation — so the trough becomes a bowl, descend there, and convert the answer back.

text:
15.12 Task 4 — Make it converge
Standardise, descend with a learning rate a thousand times larger, and rescale the parameters to the original units.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

zx <- (glu$age - mean(glu$age)) / sd(glu$age)
zy <- (glu$glucose - ______) / sd(glu$glucose)

std <- descend_mse(zx, zy, alpha = 0.1, n = 50)

slope     <- std$b1 * sd(glu$glucose) / sd(glu$age)
intercept <- mean(glu$glucose) + sd(glu$glucose) * std$b0 - slope * mean(glu$age)

c(intercept = intercept, slope = slope)
check_matches(slope, coef(lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu))[["age"]],
              label = "slope from gradient descent")







TipStuck?





Standardising a column means centring it on its own mean and dividing by its own standard deviation. The line above does it for age; do the same thing to glucose.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

mx, sx = glu["age"].mean(), glu["age"].std()
my, sy = glu["glucose"].mean(), glu["glucose"].std()
zx = (glu["age"] - mx) / sx
zy = (glu["glucose"] - ______) / sy

std = descend_mse(zx, zy, alpha=0.1, n=50)

slope     = std["b1"] * sy / sx
intercept = my + sy * std["b0"] - slope * mx

ref = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"])
print(intercept, slope)
check_matches(slope, ref.coef_[0], label="slope from gradient descent")




Fifty iterations on the standardised data give 110.298 and 0.28867, agreeing with lm() to five significant figures. The same algorithm, the same data, the same loss; twenty times fewer iterations and a thousand times larger step. Scaling was not a tidying-up step, it was the difference between an answer and no answer.






NoteOne more thing the standardised fit tells you



On standardised columns the fitted slope is 0.1347, which is exactly the correlation between age and glucose. That is not a coincidence, and Chapter 16 shows why.



RPython



std_shown <- descend_mse((glu$age - mean(glu$age)) / sd(glu$age),
                         (glu$glucose - mean(glu$glucose)) / sd(glu$glucose),
                         alpha = 0.1, n = 50)

data.frame(iteration = 1:50, MSE = std_shown$mse) |>
  ggplot(aes(iteration, MSE)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "MSE (standardised units)")











std_shown = descend_mse((glu["age"] - glu["age"].mean()) / glu["age"].std(),
                        (glu["glucose"] - glu["glucose"].mean()) / glu["glucose"].std(),
                        alpha=0.1, n=50)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(range(1, 51), std_shown["mse"], color="firebrick")
ax.set_xlabel("Iteration"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE (standardised units)")
plt.show()











That curve is the plot to draw every time you run an optimiser. A descent that is working looks like this: a steep fall, then a flat tail. Anything else — a rise, a wobble, a straight line still sloping down at the last iteration — is telling you to change the learning rate or the number of steps.

title: 15  Exercise 3.3 — Gradient descent
section: 15.15 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
15.15 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can minimise a function numerically in either language, diagnose a learning rate from the loss curve, and state why a converged descent on a convex loss gives the same answer as lm().
Cannot: that you needed any of this for linear regression. For this particular model there is an exact formula, obtainable with algebra and no iteration at all, and that is Chapter 16.

title: 16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols
text:
16.2 Why this, here
Chapter 15 minimised the squared-error loss by walking downhill, and needed standardised columns and a well-chosen learning rate to get there. For this particular loss and this particular model, none of that is necessary: the minimum can be written down. This exercise does the algebra, and then checks it against the software.






NoteThis exercise is one language, deliberately



The derivation is algebra and has no R version or Python version. Only the verification at the end is code, and that appears in both languages. If you are following the booklet in Python, the three pages of mathematics below still apply to you in full — LinearRegression is solving the same equations as lm().
crumbs: Day 3 — Fitting a line, and why it fits
16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols

title: 16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols
text:
16.3 Setting up the minimisation problem
We want the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals:
\[\min_{\hat{\beta_0}, \hat{\beta_1}} \; W, \qquad\text{where}\qquad
W = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i)^2 \tag{16.1}\]
Minimising the sum and minimising the mean are the same problem: dividing by \(N\) scales the whole surface without moving its lowest point. We use the sum here because it keeps the algebra clean.
A minimum of a smooth function is where all its partial derivatives vanish. There are two parameters, so there are two equations.
\[\frac{\partial W}{\partial \hat{\beta_0}} =
\sum_{i=1}^{N} -2(y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0 \tag{16.2}\]
\[\frac{\partial W}{\partial \hat{\beta_1}} =
\sum_{i=1}^{N} -2 x_i (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0 \tag{16.3}\]
Both follow from the chain rule: the inside of the bracket differentiates to \(-1\) with respect to \(\hat\beta_0\) and to \(-x_i\) with respect to \(\hat\beta_1\). These two are the normal equations, and everything below is rearrangement.






NoteWhere the gradients of Chapter 15 came from



Equation 16.2 and Equation 16.3, divided by \(N\), are exactly the two gradients the descent loop used. The difference between the two exercises is not the mathematics; it is that here we set the derivatives to zero and solve, while there we evaluated them at the current guess and took a step.
crumbs: Day 3 — Fitting a line, and why it fits
16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols

title: 16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols
text:
16.4 Solving for \(\hat{\beta_0}\)
Divide Equation 16.2 by \(-2\) — which is allowed because the right-hand side is zero, and is the reason some textbooks write the loss with a \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in front:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0\]
Distribute the summation over the three terms. The middle one is a constant summed \(N\) times:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - N\hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
N \hat{\beta_0} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\]
Divide by \(N\) and use \(\frac{1}{N}\sum y_i = \bar{y}\) and \(\frac{1}{N}\sum x_i = \bar{x}\):
\[\boxed{\;\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\;}\]
Read that before going on: whatever the slope turns out to be, the fitted line passes through the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). The mean of the predictors and the mean of the outcome are always on the line.
crumbs: Day 3 — Fitting a line, and why it fits
16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols

title: 16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols
text:
16.5 Solving for \(\hat{\beta_1}\)
Divide Equation 16.3 by \(-2\) as well, and expand:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( x_i y_i - \hat{\beta_0} x_i - \hat{\beta_1} x_i^2 \right) = 0\]
Substitute \(\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\) from above:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(\bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x})x_i
- \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 = 0\]
Distribute the sums, pulling the constants \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) out in front:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_i
+ \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i - \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 = 0\]
Now collect the two terms in \(\hat{\beta_1}\) on one side and use \(\sum x_i = N\bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = N\bar{y}\):
\[\hat{\beta_1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - N\bar{x}^2\right)
= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
which, using the identity in the callout below for both sides, is
\[\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}
{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}\]






NoteThe identity, in six steps





\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 1 — expand the product. \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})
= \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( x_i y_i - x_i \bar{y} - \bar{x} y_i + \bar{x} \bar{y} \right)\]
Step 2 — separate the summation. \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \bar{y}
  - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} y_i + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 3 — factor the constants out. \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) do not depend on \(i\), so \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \bar{y} = \bar{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i, \qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} y_i = \bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i, \qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} \bar{y} = N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 4 — substitute back. \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i
  - \bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i + N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 5 — use \(\sum x_i = N \bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = N \bar{y}\). \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y} (N \bar{x}) - \bar{x} (N \bar{y})
  + N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 6 — combine. The second and third terms are each \(-N\bar{x}\bar{y}\), and one of them cancels the fourth: \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Setting \(y = x\) gives the companion identity \(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \sum x_i^2 - N\bar{x}^2\), which is the denominator.



So the complete solution, for one predictor, is two lines of arithmetic:
\[\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}
\qquad\qquad
\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\]
No iteration, no learning rate, no starting guess. The derivation follows the one in Berkeley’s EEP118 handout; with more than one predictor the same argument is done in matrix form and gives \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\), which is what lm() actually evaluates.

text:
16.6 Task 1 — The closed form against the software
Compute both estimators from means, a covariance and a variance, and compare them with the fitted model.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(readr); library(dplyr)
source("checks/checks.R")

diab <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu  <- diab |> filter(glucose > 0) |> slice(1:80) |> select(age, glucose)
x    <- glu$age
y    <- glu$glucose

b1hat <- ______ / ______
b0hat <- mean(y) - b1hat * ______

fit <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)
rbind(closed_form = c(b0hat, b1hat), lm = coef(fit))

check_matches(b1hat, coef(fit)[["age"]], tol = 1e-8, label = "closed-form slope")







TipStuck?





Two functions, cov() and var(), in the order the formula gives them. The third blank is the mean of the predictor.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80).reset_index(drop=True))
x, y = glu["age"], glu["glucose"]

b1hat = ______ / ______          # pandas: x.cov(y) and x.var(), both ddof=1
b0hat = y.mean() - b1hat * ______

fit = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], y)
print({"closed_form": (b0hat, b1hat), "sklearn": (fit.intercept_, fit.coef_[0])})

check_matches(b1hat, fit.coef_[0], tol=1e-8, label="closed-form slope")




Both give 110.298 and 0.2886749. Not approximately: to every digit either language will print. lm() is not doing anything you have not just done by hand, and neither is LinearRegression.






NoteThe covariance ratio also explains Chapter 15



Standardising both columns makes \(\operatorname{Var}(x) = 1\) and turns \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)\) into the correlation, so on standardised data \(\hat\beta_1 = \operatorname{Cor}(x,y)\) — the 0.1347 the descent converged to. The correlation is the slope of the standardised fit, which is a more useful definition of it than the one most people carry.

16.7 Task 2 — The two conditions the derivation imposes
Equation 16.2 and Equation 16.3 say that at the optimum, \(\sum r_i = 0\) and \(\sum x_i r_i = 0\). Those are not assumptions about the world; they are consequences of having minimised. Check both for the fitted line, and for the hand-drawn line from Chapter 14.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
r_fitted <- ______                     # residuals of the fitted line
r_guess  <- y - (120 + 0.5 * x)        # residuals of the hand-drawn line

rbind(fitted = c(sum_r = sum(r_fitted), sum_xr = sum(x * r_fitted)),
      guess  = c(sum_r = sum(r_guess),  sum_xr = sum(x * r_guess)))

check_matches(sum(r_fitted), 0, tol = 1e-6, label = "sum of fitted residuals")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
r_fitted = ______                      # residuals of the fitted line
r_guess  = y - (120 + 0.5 * x)

print({"fitted": (r_fitted.sum(), (x * r_fitted).sum()),
       "guess":  (r_guess.sum(),  (x * r_guess).sum())})

check_matches(r_fitted.sum(), 0, tol=1e-6, label="sum of fitted residuals")




The fitted residuals sum to something of the order of \(10^{-13}\) and their product with age to the order of \(10^{-11}\): zero, to the precision floating-point arithmetic allows. The hand-drawn line’s residuals sum to −1338.5 and its cross-product to −47700.5.
That is a diagnostic worth keeping. If someone hands you fitted values from a least-squares model and the residuals do not sum to zero, either there is no intercept in the model or those are not least-squares fitted values.

title: 16  Exercise 3.4 — Ols
section: 16.8 The result that should bother you
text:
16.8 The result that should bother you
The derivation divides by \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\). It therefore returns an answer for any dataset in which the predictor is not perfectly constant — and says nothing about how large that variance is. Refit the same model on progressively narrower age bands.

RPython



bands <- list(c(21, 25), c(21, 30), c(21, 40), c(21, 81))

do.call(rbind, lapply(bands, function(b) {
  s <- glu |> filter(age >= b[1], age <= b[2])
  data.frame(band = paste(b[1], "to", b[2]), n = nrow(s),
             var_age = var(s$age),
             slope = cov(s$age, s$glucose) / var(s$age))
}))

#>       band  n    var_age     slope
#> 1 21 to 25 32   1.910282 0.6812665
#> 2 21 to 30 48   8.074025 4.1727148
#> 3 21 to 40 59  21.303916 2.2139585
#> 4 21 to 81 80 190.398576 0.2886749





rows = []
for lo, hi in [(21, 25), (21, 30), (21, 40), (21, 81)]:
    s = glu[(glu["age"] >= lo) & (glu["age"] <= hi)]
    rows.append({"band": f"{lo} to {hi}", "n": len(s),
                 "var_age": s["age"].var(),
                 "slope": s["age"].cov(s["glucose"]) / s["age"].var()})
pd.DataFrame(rows)

#>        band   n     var_age     slope
#> 0  21 to 25  32    1.910282  0.681266
#> 1  21 to 30  48    8.074025  4.172715
#> 2  21 to 40  59   21.303916  2.213958
#> 3  21 to 81  80  190.398576  0.288675





Three steps of reasoning.

Over the full range the slope is 0.289 mg/dL per year. Among patients aged 21 to 40 it is 2.21, and among those aged 21 to 30 it is 4.17 — fourteen times the full-range estimate, from a subset of the same 80 patients.
The mechanism is the denominator. Restricting the age range cuts \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\) from 190 to 8, and the covariance in the numerator is estimated from fewer, closer points, so it is noise-dominated. The estimator is behaving exactly as derived; the data cannot support what is being asked of it.
So a published slope is not a property of a relationship. It is a property of a relationship and the range of predictor values the sample happened to cover. When you compare your coefficient with someone else’s, compare the predictor ranges first.

title: 17  Day 3 — Consolidation
text:
17.4 Five questions
Answer in a sentence each.

A colleague fits glucose on age, reports a slope of 0.29, and concludes that age does not matter clinically. Give two separate reasons that conclusion is not supported — one about the number, one about what was never computed.
Tripling three glucose readings out of 80 flipped the fitted slope from positive to negative, while the least-absolute-error line did not move at all. Which of the two lines is correct?
Your gradient descent reports a loss that fell at every iteration and parameters that are nowhere near lm()’s. What has happened, and what is the first thing you change?
The OLS derivation divides by \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\). What happens to the estimate as that variance shrinks, and what does that imply about comparing a coefficient from a narrow age band with one from a wide one?
If lm() solves the problem exactly in microseconds, why does any software use gradient descent at all?

title: 17  Day 3 — Consolidation
text:
17.5 What carries into Day 4
Three loose ends were left deliberately, and each opens the next session.

Every number today was in-sample. No split, no held-out patient, no evidence of generalisation. Day 5 brings the metrics back, and the tree that looked best on these 80 rows is the first casualty.
The outcome was continuous. Squared error is defined because the difference between a prediction and an outcome is a number. When the outcome is a diagnosis — positive or negative — subtraction stops meaning anything, and a new loss is needed. That is Chapter 20.
The loss was chosen for us. We showed that the choice changes the answer and then went back to squared error anyway, because it is differentiable. Day 4’s loss is chosen for the same reason, and it is worth noticing that convenience keeps winning.

title: 18  Day 4 — Overview
text:
18.1 Objectives
Days 1 to 3 predicted a number and scored it with an average error. Today the outcome is a class — this patient has diabetes or does not — and two things change. The model stops emitting a prediction and starts emitting a probability; and somebody, at some point, has to turn that probability into an action. That second step is not part of the model, it is not chosen by the software, and it is where most of the clinical consequences live. Chapter 3 ended with a loose end that today picks up: a decision is not a prediction.
Along the way we stop hand-writing each model’s own syntax and move to the two frameworks the rest of the module uses, tidymodels and scikit-learn.
By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

19.2 Why this, here
In Chapter 3 you wrote the five steps out by hand, with lm() in R and LinearRegression() in Python. That is affordable for one model. From today the models multiply — logistic regression now, trees and forests on Chapter 23 — and each one of them has its own function name, its own argument names and its own way of returning a prediction. rpart() wants method = "class"; randomForest() wants the outcome to be a factor and will quietly do regression if it is not; glmnet() refuses a formula and demands a matrix.
Two ecosystems exist to put one interface in front of all of that: tidymodels in R and scikit-learn in Python. The point of this exercise is not that they save typing. It is that they make models comparable: when the only line that differs between two analyses is the one naming the model, the difference in the result is attributable to the model.








The question
tidymodels
scikit-learn




what kind of model is this
logistic_reg(), decision_tree()
the estimator class, LogisticRegression


which code actually fits it
set_engine("glm")
the class, plus solver=


what happens to the data first
a recipe() of step_*()
transformers, e.g. StandardScaler


the two bolted together
workflow()
Pipeline


fit it, then use it
fit(), predict()
.fit(), .predict()

title: 19  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 19.3 A specification is not a model
text:
19.3 A specification is not a model
Declaring a model and fitting it are separate acts, and both frameworks make you notice. In R you can print a specification that has never seen data. In Python the estimator exists, but asking it to predict raises an error until you fit it.

RPython



library(tidymodels)

log_spec  <- logistic_reg(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("glm")
tree_spec <- decision_tree(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("rpart")

log_spec

#> Logistic Regression Model Specification (classification)
#> 
#> Computational engine: glm





from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.exceptions import NotFittedError

log_spec = LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)

try:
    log_spec.predict([[120.0, 30.0, 40.0]])
except NotFittedError as e:
    print(str(e).split(".")[0])

#> This LogisticRegression instance is not fitted yet





The R specification says logistic regression, fitted by glm and nothing else: no data, no coefficients. Swapping "glm" for "glmnet" keeps the first half and replaces the second.

section: 19.4 The split we use all day
text:
19.4 The split we use all day
data/diabetes.csv holds 768 patients: eight measurements and diabetes, which is pos or neg. It is the synthetic replacement for the withdrawn Pima Indians data — read Section B.5 before you quote a number from it anywhere.
We hold back every fifth row. That is not how you would usually split, and the reason we do it here is worth a paragraph.






NoteWhy a fixed rule rather than a seed



Chapter 3 showed that set.seed(42) and random_state=42 select different rows, so the two languages ended the day with different test sets and different scores. That is honest, but it means any R-versus-Python difference you then see is confounded with the split.
Taking every fifth row of a file whose row order carries no information gives both languages the same 153 patients, so the rest of this day compares languages rather than partitions. Exercise 1.2’s Stretch 2 asked how much the split matters; Stretch 1 below is that question again, and the answer is still “more than you would like”.



RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test), test_pos = sum(test$diabetes == "pos"))

#>    train     test test_pos 
#>      615      153       55





import pandas as pd

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")

is_test = (diabetes.index + 1) % 5 == 0
train, test = diabetes[~is_test], diabetes[is_test]

y_train = (train["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
y_test  = (test["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
features = ["glucose", "mass", "age"]

len(train), len(test), int(y_test.sum())

#> (615, 153, 55)

title: 19  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 19.5 Fit and predict: the same two verbs, whatever the model
text:
19.5 Fit and predict: the same two verbs, whatever the model

RPython



log_fit  <- log_spec  |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)
tree_fit <- tree_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

acc <- function(f) mean(predict(f, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
c(logistic = acc(log_fit), tree = acc(tree_fit),
  majority = mean(test$diabetes == "neg"))

#>  logistic      tree  majority 
#> 0.7124183 0.6928105 0.6405229





from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

log_fit  = LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
tree_fit = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42).fit(train[features], y_train)

{"logistic": round(log_fit.score(test[features], y_test), 4),
 "tree":     round(tree_fit.score(test[features], y_test), 4),
 "majority": round(float((y_test == 0).mean()), 4)}

#> {'logistic': 0.7124, 'tree': 0.5948, 'majority': 0.6405}





Two readings, and the second is the uncomfortable one.
The logistic regressions agree: 0.712 in both languages, on the same 153 patients. The trees do not — about 0.69 in R against about 0.59 in Python — and the word decision_tree is identical in both. rpart stops growing when a split stops paying for itself, so it returns ten leaves; DecisionTreeClassifier grows until every leaf is pure, so it returns about 180 and scores 1.00 on the rows it was fitted to. Same name, same data, different default, and the default is the whole difference. Chapter 26 is where you learn to control it.
And a third reading, which should take the shine off all of them: always saying neg scores 0.641 on this test set. The logistic model’s seven percentage points over that is the entire return on three clinical measurements.

section: 19.6 Task 1 — Swap the model, keep everything else
text:
19.6 Task 1 — Swap the model, keep everything else
Fit a third model — a random forest, five hundred trees instead of one — on the same rows, and score it against the majority baseline. One line names the model; nothing else changes.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
rf_fit <- rand_forest(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 42) |>
  fit(______, data = ______)

acc_rf <- mean(predict(rf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, test$diabetes)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf_fit = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42).fit(______, ______)

acc_rf = rf_fit.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, y_test)










TipStuck?





The R side wants the same formula and the same data frame you gave fit() for the logistic model. The Python side wants the predictor columns and the outcome as two separate arguments — that is the shape difference from Exercise 1.1, and it has not gone away.



A forest has no coefficients, no equation and no way of telling a clinician why it said what it said. It also, here, does not win: five hundred trees score about 0.69–0.70 against the logistic regression’s 0.712 on the same rows. Note that down before Chapter 27, and note too that the cost of finding it out was one line — which is the argument for the framework, and the only argument this exercise is making.

section: 19.7 Task 2 — Swap the engine, keep the model
text:
19.7 Task 2 — Swap the engine, keep the model
Now change only the second half of the specification. In R, replace the glm engine with glmnet, which fits the same logistic model with a penalty on the coefficients. In Python there is no engine slot; the nearest thing is solver=, so change that instead and see whether it does the same job.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
lasso_fit <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("______") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

round(coef(lasso_fit$fit, s = 0.1)[, 1], 5)   # compare with the glm coefficients
round(coef(log_fit$fit), 5)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import numpy as np
for solver in ["lbfgs", "newton-cg", "______"]:
    m = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, solver=solver, max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
    print(f"{solver:>10}", np.round(m.coef_[0], 5), round(m.intercept_[0], 3))




In R the engine change is a change of model: the lasso drives the coefficients for mass and age to exactly zero and keeps only glucose. Two of your three predictors have left the building, and nothing in the specification said they could.
In Python two of the three solvers agree to four decimal places and the third, liblinear, does not — it penalises the intercept as well, which the other two do not. So “the solver is only a numerical detail” is true twice out of three times, which is the worst possible number of times for a thing to be true.

section: 19.8 Task 3 — Put preprocessing inside the model object
text:
19.8 Task 3 — Put preprocessing inside the model object
A workflow and a Pipeline are the same idea: one object that remembers both what you did to the data and what you fitted to it, so that the identical treatment reaches the test rows. Build one with the predictors standardised.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
rec <- recipe(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train) |>
  step_normalize(______)

wf_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_model(log_spec) |>
  add_recipe(______) |>
  fit(data = train)

acc_wf <- mean(predict(wf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_wf, test$diabetes)
round(coef(extract_fit_engine(wf_fit)), 4)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", ______),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)),
]).fit(train[features], y_train)

acc_pipe = pipe.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_pipe, y_test)
np.round(pipe[-1].coef_[0], 4), round(pipe[-1].intercept_[0], 4)










NoteAssign the result of .fit(), always



Written as a bare line, pipe.fit(X, y) returns the fitted pipeline, and both Jupyter and this booklet will then print scikit-learn’s HTML representation of it — the grey box listing every default parameter. It is noise in a notebook, and in a knitr render under a non-UTF-8 locale it stops the build outright. Assign the result, or end the line with a semicolon.


Compare the standardised coefficients with the unstandardised ones from the earlier cell. The accuracy is unchanged at 0.712 — an unpenalised logistic regression does not care about the units of its predictors — but the coefficients now say something the originals could not: per standard deviation, glucose carries about four times the weight of mass or age.






NoteTwo things differ between the languages here, and only one matters



R reports the standardised glucose coefficient as about 1.1804 and Python as about 1.1794. The cause is that step_normalize() divides by the sample standard deviation (dividing by \(n-1\)) and StandardScaler by the population one (dividing by \(n\)). It is a convention, it is a fourth decimal place, and it never changed a clinical conclusion.
The difference that does matter is in the next section.
The reason to put the scaling inside the object rather than before the split is leakage: a scaler fitted on all 768 rows has read the test set’s mean. That is Chapter 10’s subject and this is the machinery that prevents it.

title: 19  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 19.9 The result that should bother you
text:
19.9 The result that should bother you
The two frameworks give you the same interface. They do not give you the same model.

On these 615 training rows, R’s glm and scikit-learn with C=inf agree to five decimal places: glucose 0.03508, mass 0.03598, age 0.02170. Whatever else is going on, the two libraries solve the same problem when you ask them to.
But C=inf is not scikit-learn’s default. The default is C=1.0, which is an L2 penalty on the coefficients — the thing the glmnet engine does in R only when you ask for it. On 615 rows the penalty is swamped by the likelihood and you cannot see it.
Run the cell below, which refits on the first 50 rows only. Now you can.


RPython



small <- diabetes[1:50, ]
z <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
glm_small <- glm(diabetes ~ z(glucose) + z(mass) + z(age) + z(pedigree),
                 data = small, family = binomial)
round(coef(glm_small), 3)

#> (Intercept)  z(glucose)     z(mass)      z(age) z(pedigree) 
#>      -1.118       0.799      -0.022       0.101       0.968





from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

small = diabetes.iloc[:50]
y_small = (small["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
f4 = ["glucose", "mass", "age", "pedigree"]

for C, label in [(float("inf"), "no penalty"), (1.0, "the default")]:
    p = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()),
                  ("model", LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=2000))]).fit(small[f4], y_small)
    print(f"{label:>12}", dict(zip(f4, np.round(p[-1].coef_[0], 3))))

#>   no penalty {'glucose': np.float64(0.791), 'mass': np.float64(-0.022), 'age': np.float64(0.1), 'pedigree': np.float64(0.959)}
#>  the default {'glucose': np.float64(0.663), 'mass': np.float64(0.035), 'age': np.float64(0.117), 'pedigree': np.float64(0.751)}





Unpenalised, mass has a coefficient of −0.022; at the default C=1.0 it is +0.035. Fifty patients, four predictors, and the sign of a clinical association depends on an argument nobody typed. R’s unpenalised glm gives −0.022 too: it matches the unpenalised Python fit, not Python’s default.
The lesson is not that scikit-learn is wrong — a penalty on 50 rows is good statistics, and Day 5 will argue for it. The lesson is that “I fitted a logistic regression” does not identify a model, and a methods section that says only that cannot be reproduced in the other language.

NoteStretch 1 — How much of today is the split?



Replace the every-fifth-row rule with initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8, strata = diabetes) under ten different seeds, and collect the ten logistic accuracies. Ours ran from about 0.69 to 0.80. The majority baseline moves too. Report the range, and then decide what you think of a paper that reports one split and three decimal places.

Grow the scikit-learn tree with ccp_alpha=0.01 and refit. The test accuracy rises from about 0.59 to about 0.71. You have not changed the algorithm, the data or the split — only the default that decides when to stop. Keep the number: Chapter 26 is about why pruning is the whole game.

title: 19  Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models
section: 19.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
19.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that you can fit, swap and score models through one interface in either language, and that you know which line to change to swap the algorithm, the engine or the preprocessing.
Cannot: that any of these models is any good. Every number on this page is an accuracy, and accuracy on a 36% prevalence outcome is a weak instrument — 0.641 of it is free. Before judging a classifier you need to know what it predicts for an individual patient, which is a probability, and that is Chapter 20.

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
text:
20.2 Why this, here
Chapter 19 fitted four classifiers and scored them all with accuracy, which is a property of a whole test set. No clinician has ever treated a test set. The object a clinician meets is a single patient with a single number attached, and for logistic regression that number is a probability — which is why this is the model the booklet uses to learn classification, long before the more accurate ones.
Getting from a linear model to a probability needs one idea, and the idea is arithmetic rather than statistics.
crumbs: Day 4 — Predicting a class, and choosing a threshold
20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
text:
20.3 Probability, odds, log-odds

RPython



p <- 0.8
odds <- p / (1 - p)
logit <- log(odds)
c(probability = p, odds = odds, log_odds = logit)

#> probability        odds    log_odds 
#>    0.800000    4.000000    1.386294





import numpy as np

p = 0.8
odds = p / (1 - p)
logit = np.log(odds)
{"probability": p, "odds": odds, "log_odds": round(float(logit), 4)}

#> {'probability': 0.8, 'odds': 4.000000000000001, 'log_odds': 1.3863}





Three names for the same belief, on three different scales.

A probability lives in \([0, 1]\).
The odds, \(p/(1-p)\), live in \([0, \infty)\). A probability of 0.8 is odds of 4, usually said as “four to one on”.
The log-odds or logit, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)\), live on the whole real line.

Only the third is a scale a linear model can safely be written on: a linear predictor is unbounded, and so are the log-odds. That single sentence is the whole reason logistic regression has the form it does.
\[\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
and running it backwards gives the logistic (sigmoid) function
\[p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}.\]






NoteThis bit has no language



The two equations above are algebra, so there is no R version and no Python version of them. Everything below is both. Deriving the second from the first takes three lines and is the only derivation in today’s material; do it once, on paper, and you will never again be unsure which way round exp goes.

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 20.4 Fit it, in both languages, to the same rows
text:
20.4 Fit it, in both languages, to the same rows
data/diabetes.csv again (Section B.5), all 768 patients, one predictor. We are not splitting here, and the reason is not laziness: this exercise reads the shape of a fitted curve and the meaning of a coefficient, neither of which is a claim about unseen patients. The moment we make such a claim — the next exercise — the split comes back.

RPython



library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

fit_glucose <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = diabetes)

tidy(fit_glucose)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)  -5.10     0.400       -12.8 3.09e-37
#> 2 glucose       0.0355   0.00302      11.8 5.89e-32





import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X = diabetes[["glucose"]]

fit_glucose = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
float(fit_glucose.intercept_[0]), float(fit_glucose.coef_[0][0])

#> (-5.0953569044194404, 0.03548515592234879)





Both give an intercept of −5.09536 and a glucose coefficient of 0.035485. They agree to every digit printed because they are now solving the same problem: C=np.inf switches off the L2 penalty that scikit-learn applies by default, and which R’s glm never applies at all (Chapter 19).






WarningC=np.inf, and what to do if your scikit-learn complains



Older versions of scikit-learn spell the same thing penalty=None, and versions from 1.8 deprecate that spelling in favour of C=np.inf. If you leave the argument out altogether you will get a slightly different, penalised fit and the two languages will stop agreeing — on this dataset in the fourth decimal place, on a small one in the first.


The fitted model is therefore
\[\operatorname{logit}\big(P(\text{diabetes} = \text{pos} \mid \text{glucose})\big)
= -5.095 + 0.0355 \times \text{glucose}.\]

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 20.5 Task 1 — Say the coefficient out loud
text:
20.5 Task 1 — Say the coefficient out loud
A log-odds coefficient is not interpretable as it stands, and 0.0355 per mg/dL is not a sentence anyone would say. Exponentiating turns it into an odds ratio, and a 10 mg/dL step is a clinically sensible unit. Produce the odds ratio for a 10 mg/dL rise in glucose.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
beta_glucose <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]]
or_10 <- ______(10 * beta_glucose)
check_metric_range(or_10, 1.2, 1.7, "odds ratio per 10 mg/dL")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
beta_glucose = fit_glucose.coef_[0][0]
or_10 = ______(10 * beta_glucose)
check_metric_range(or_10, 1.2, 1.7, "odds ratio per 10 mg/dL")










TipStuck?





The coefficient is on the log-odds scale and you want the odds scale. One function undoes a logarithm.



Write the sentence the number supports, in full: every 10 mg/dL of glucose multiplies the odds of diabetes by about 1.43. Then write what it does not support. It is not a risk ratio, it is not an effect of glucose on anything, and it is not a 43% increase in the probability — which the next task makes uncomfortably concrete.

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 20.6 Task 2 — One patient, by hand and by machine
text:
20.6 Task 2 — One patient, by hand and by machine
A patient presents with a glucose of 120. Compute their log-odds, odds and probability from the two coefficients, using nothing but arithmetic. Then ask the fitted object for the same probability and check the two agree.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
b <- coef(fit_glucose$fit)

log_odds_120 <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["glucose"]] * ______
odds_120     <- exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     <- 1 / (1 + exp(______))

by_machine <- predict(fit_glucose,
                      new_data = tibble(glucose = 120),
                      type = "prob")$.pred_pos

round(c(log_odds = log_odds_120, odds = odds_120,
        prob = prob_120, by_machine = by_machine), 4)
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
b0, b1 = fit_glucose.intercept_[0], fit_glucose.coef_[0][0]

log_odds_120 = b0 + b1 * ______
odds_120     = np.exp(log_odds_120)
prob_120     = 1 / (1 + np.exp(______))

by_machine = fit_glucose.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"glucose": [120]}))[0, 1]

print(np.round([log_odds_120, odds_120, prob_120, by_machine], 4))
check_metric_range(prob_120, 0.25, 0.35, "P(pos | glucose = 120)")




The answer is a probability of about 0.302: log-odds −0.837, odds 0.433. Now compare it with the sentence from Task 1. The odds ratio of 1.43 per 10 mg/dL is constant for every patient; the change in probability for the same 10 mg/dL is not. Going from 120 to 130 moves the probability by about 8 percentage points; going from 60 to 70 moves it by about 2. The model is linear in the log-odds and in nothing else, which is exactly what the sigmoid’s shape is telling you.

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 20.7 Task 3 — Draw the curve over the data
text:
20.7 Task 3 — Draw the curve over the data
Plot the predicted probability against glucose, with the observed outcomes drawn at 0 and 1 underneath. This is the plot to have in your head whenever anyone says “the model predicts diabetes”.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(ggplot2)
preds <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(diabetes) |>
  mutate(observed = if_else(diabetes == "pos", ______, 0))

ggplot(preds, aes(x = glucose)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ______), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Observed class (0/1) and P(pos)")




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
diabetes["p_pos"] = fit_glucose.predict_proba(X)[:, ______]
ordered = diabetes.sort_values("glucose")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(diabetes["glucose"], y, alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(ordered["glucose"], ordered["p_pos"], color="red")
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)"); ax.set_ylabel("Observed class (0/1) and P(pos)")
plt.show()










TipStuck?





In R the probability of the event is the column predict(type = "prob") named after the level you want. In Python predict_proba returns one column per class, in the order given by the estimator’s classes_ attribute — print it before you choose an index.



Two features of this plot deserve a sentence each. The curve never reaches 0 or 1: at the lowest real glucose in the file, 57 mg/dL, the model still gives 0.044, and it will not tell you a patient is safe. And there are five points at glucose = 0, which is not a glucose a living patient has; the file codes some missing values as zeros, which Chapter 8 takes apart.

section: 20.8 Task 4 — Which column did you take?
text:
20.8 Task 4 — Which column did you take?
Half of all logistic regression errors are taking the probability of the wrong class. There is a check for it, and the reason the check works is worth knowing: a logistic regression with an intercept, scored on the rows it was fitted to, produces fitted probabilities whose mean equals the observed prevalence exactly. Take the other column and you get one minus it.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
p_pos <- predict(fit_glucose, new_data = diabetes, type = "prob")$______
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence = mean(diabetes$diabetes == "pos"))




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
print("classes_:", fit_glucose.classes_)
p_pos = fit_glucose.predict_proba(X)[:, ______]
check_probabilities(p_pos, prevalence=float(y.mean()))




Run it deliberately wrong once — take .pred_neg, or column 0 — and read what the check says. A check you have never seen fail is a check you do not trust.

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 20.9 The result that should bother you
text:
20.9 The result that should bother you
The original course notes for this material relevel the outcome so that pos comes first, on the reasonable grounds that pos is the event of interest. Do that, and the coefficient on glucose becomes negative, while the predicted probability of diabetes for every patient stays exactly the same.

library(forcats)
relevelled <- diabetes |> mutate(diabetes = fct_relevel(diabetes, "pos"))
fit_relevelled <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = relevelled)

round(c(original   = coef(fit_glucose$fit)[["glucose"]],
        relevelled = coef(fit_relevelled$fit)[["glucose"]]), 5)

#>   original relevelled 
#>    0.03549   -0.03549

p_orig <- predict(fit_glucose,    new_data = diabetes,   type = "prob")$.pred_pos
p_relv <- predict(fit_relevelled, new_data = relevelled, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
max(abs(p_orig - p_relv))

#> [1] 1.110223e-15



glm() models the probability of the last level of the factor. With levels neg, pos it models pos, so the coefficient is +0.0355: more glucose, more diabetes. Relevel, and the last level is neg, so the same engine now models the probability of not having diabetes and reports −0.0355.
parsnip knows this. It asks the engine for its own event, then returns both columns correctly labelled, which is why .pred_pos is identical to fifteen decimal places either way.
So the coefficient’s sign and the column’s name follow two different conventions, and the published page that made this change kept a sentence underneath saying the model was \(\operatorname{logit}(P(\text{pos})) = \beta_0
+ \beta_1 x\). With pos relevelled first, that sentence was false and the plot above it was right.

The transferable rule: never read a sign off a coefficient without checking which class the engine thinks it is modelling. The cheap way to check is the one you already have — predict for a patient with a high glucose and see which direction the probability went.

The odds ratio is constant and the probability difference is not. Which of the two would you put in a patient-facing leaflet, and what would you have to add to make it honest?
This model has an accuracy you have not computed and a probability for every patient that you have. Which of those two would change if the study had recruited twice as many pos patients, and why does that matter for a model fitted on a case-control sample?

text:
20.11 Stretch






NoteStretch 1 — Where is the curve steepest?



Find the glucose value at which the predicted probability is 0.5, from the two coefficients alone: it is \(-\beta_0/\beta_1\). Ours is about 144 mg/dL. This is the point at which the model is least sure, and — as Chapter 21 will show — it is also exactly what you are choosing when you choose a threshold of 0.5.








NoteStretch 2 — Add a predictor, and watch the coefficient move



Refit with diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age. The glucose coefficient changes a little (0.0355 to about 0.0328) and the intercept moves a long way (−5.10 to about −6.74). Explain why the second of those is arithmetic rather than news, and what the first one would have to look like before you called glucose confounded by age.

title: 20  Exercise 4.2 — Probability, odds, and the fitted curve
section: 20.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
20.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that for a patient drawn from this population, the model gives a probability of diabetes, and that you can produce and interpret that probability on all three scales.
Cannot: that any patient has diabetes. The model has not said so and cannot: a probability is not a decision, and nothing in the fitting procedure knows what it costs to be wrong in either direction. Turning 0.302 into a yes or a no is a separate act with separate consequences, and it is Chapter 21.
