32  Exercise 6.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX

title: 32  Exercise 6.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
text:
32.3 One explainer, any model
DALEX works by wrapping the model in a uniform interface: the data, the true outcome, and a function that turns rows into predictions. Everything else is computed from that, which is why the same code works for a forest, a regression or something written by someone else entirely.

library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)
library(DALEX); library(DALEXtra); library(vip); library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
dia <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")),
         noise    = round(rnorm(n()), 2))

split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train) |>
               step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
  add_model(rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3, min_n = 10) |>
              set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity", seed = 123) |>
              set_mode("classification"))

rf_fit <- fit(rf_wf, data = train)

explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = select(test, -diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"),
  label = "random forest",
  verbose = FALSE
)







WarningRead the y argument twice



diabetes is a factor, and as.numeric() on a factor returns the level codes — 1 and 2, not 0 and 1. Pass that to explain_tidymodels() and the explainer believes every patient has an outcome of at least 1 while the model predicts probabilities below 1, so every residual is positive and the mean residual is about 1. Nothing errors. The importance plot still draws. Compare with as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"), which gives the 0/1 the explainer expects.
The diagnostic is free: print the explainer with verbose = TRUE and read the residual line. If the mean residual is not near zero, the outcome is wrong.



# the free diagnostic: residuals should straddle zero
round(summary(explainer$residuals), 3)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  -0.844  -0.291  -0.078   0.001   0.283   0.932

text:
32.4 Task 1 — Global importance, and the control for the third time
model_parts() is permutation importance: it shuffles each variable B times and records the loss. For a classification task the default loss is one minus AUC, so a variable that matters has a higher dropout loss than the full model.

set.seed(123)
mp <- model_parts(explainer, B = 20)
plot(mp)








_full_model_ marks the intact loss and _baseline_ the loss of a model that predicts the mean, so the distance between them is all the AUC the forest has. Turn the losses into drops and run the control check.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

losses <- as.data.frame(______) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(loss = mean(dropout_loss), .groups = "drop")
full   <- losses$loss[losses$variable == "_full_model_"]
drops  <- setNames(losses$loss - ______, losses$variable)
drops  <- drops[!names(drops) %in% c("_baseline_", "_full_model_")]

round(sort(drops, decreasing = TRUE), 4)
check_noise_control(drops)







TipStuck?





The quantity you want is each variable’s mean loss minus the loss of the intact model, which is the row model_parts() labels _full_model_. The object to summarise is the one you just plotted.



The picture matches Python’s to the extent that you should expect: glucose far ahead, age second, everything else in an undifferentiated band, and the control inside that band at a few per cent of glucose.

32.5 Partial dependence — the average patient who does not exist
A partial dependence profile asks: if I set this variable to \(v\) for every patient in the data, leaving all their other values alone, what does the model predict on average? Sweep \(v\) across the observed range and you get a curve.

pdp_glucose  <- model_profile(explainer, variable = "glucose",  type = "partial")
pdp_pedigree <- model_profile(explainer, variable = "pedigree", type = "partial")
plot(pdp_glucose, pdp_pedigree)








Glucose moves the average prediction from about 0.19 to about 0.74 across its range — a real and large effect. Pedigree moves it very little, and most of what movement there is sits at the sparse right-hand end of the variable.

32.7 Local explanation — the same patient, a different algorithm
predict_parts(type = "shap") computes Shapley values by sampling orderings of the variables, rather than exploiting the tree structure as TreeExplainer does. It is slower and approximate, and it works for models that are not trees.

patient <- test[1, setdiff(names(test), "diabetes")]
patient

#> # A tibble: 1 × 9
#>   pregnant glucose pressure triceps insulin  mass pedigree   age noise
#>      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1        8     129       84       0       0  27.6    0.828    44 -0.23

cat("predicted:", round(predict(explainer, patient), 3),
    " actual:", as.character(test$diabetes[1]), "\n")

#> predicted: 0.655  actual: pos

set.seed(123)
local_shap <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = patient,
                            type = "shap", B = 25)
plot(local_shap)








The bars are the same quantity as Chapter 31’s force plot, drawn differently and estimated by a different algorithm. The boxplots behind them are the spread across the 25 sampled orderings — a feature the Python plot does not show you, and a useful reminder that these contributions are estimates with uncertainty unless your model is a tree ensemble.

title: 32  Exercise 6.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX
section: 32.9 The result that should bother you
text:
32.9 The result that should bother you
Ask for a partial dependence profile of insulin.

# the profile averages the model over the explainer's data, which is the test set
cat("rows with insulin recorded as 0:",
    sum(test$insulin == 0), "of", nrow(test), "\n")

#> rows with insulin recorded as 0: 130 of 231

cat("largest observed insulin:", max(test$insulin), "\n")

#> largest observed insulin: 846

plot(model_profile(explainer, variable = "insulin", type = "partial"))








It is a smooth, gently rising curve, and it is nonsense. Three steps.

More than half the rows the profile averages over record insulin as exactly zero, which is not a measurement — it is a missing value written as a number, the defect you met in Chapter 8. The curve’s left-hand end is the model’s behaviour on “not measured”, plotted as though it were a concentration.
The curve’s right-hand end sets insulin to its maximum for every patient, including the ones whose insulin was never measured and the ones for whom that combination of values is physiologically impossible. Partial dependence averages the model over rows that do not exist and could not exist.
So the curve is well defined as a property of the fitted function, and it is not an answer to “what happens if insulin rises”. That question is causal, and nothing on this page can answer it.

The same objection applies, more weakly, to every other partial dependence plot you will ever be shown. Variables are correlated; holding the others fixed while moving one walks you off the data.

section: 32.12 What you can and cannot now claim
text:
32.12 What you can and cannot now claim
Can: that this forest, explained in R by three methods, tells the same story as the Python explanations of Chapter 31 — glucose dominates, nothing else is clearly separated from the control, and the model’s own impurity importance disagrees with all of it.
Cannot: that any of this is evidence about diabetes. Every figure on this page is a description of a function that was fitted to 537 rows of one synthetic file. What that function has to do with patients is a question none of today’s tools can be made to answer — which is where Chapter 33 leaves you.

title: 33  Day 6 — Consolidation
text:
33.1 Say it in one sentence
20 minutes · plenary
An explanation is a statement about the model. It is not a statement about the patient, and it is not evidence about the disease.
Everything today was a demonstration of that sentence. A column of random numbers was ranked fifth of nine by the forest’s own importance measure, and the model was no worse without it. A force plot gave a faithful, exact account of a predicted probability of 0.71 for a woman who did not have diabetes. A forest fitted to shuffled labels, scoring an AUC of 0.47, produced a SHAP summary as orderly as the real one. A partial dependence curve for insulin ran smoothly across values that, for half the patients, were never measured.
None of those figures was wrong. Each was a correct answer to a question about a fitted function, read as though it were an answer to a question about people.

33.2 Self-assessment

I can say what impurity importance measures, and why a pure-noise column scores highly on it.
I can say what permutation importance measures, and why it needs held-out rows.
I can state the SHAP additivity identity and check it in code.
I can read a beeswarm plot and a force plot aloud without making a claim about the patient.

I can build a DALEX explainer around a tidymodels workflow and check that it has the outcome the right way round.

title: 33  Day 6 — Consolidation
text:
33.3 Questions

Two importance measures rank the same model’s variables differently. Your collaborator asks which is correct. Answer in two sentences.
You are shown a beeswarm plot for a model you did not fit. Name the two things you must know before you read anything off it.
A patient’s force plot shows glucose contributing +0.31. She asks whether lowering her glucose would lower her risk. What do you say?
noise scored 37% of glucose under impurity importance, 12% under mean absolute SHAP, and about zero under permutation importance. Put those three numbers in order of how much they tell you about the data, and justify the order.
You have a model with an AUC of 0.47 and a beautiful SHAP summary. What is the correct next action, and what would be the wrong one?

title: 33  Day 6 — Consolidation
section: 33.4 What carries out of the module
text:
33.4 What carries out of the module
Three loose ends were left deliberately, and all three are where this material goes next.

Explanation is not causation, and today had no way to close that gap. Everything on Day 6 describes a fitted function. The question clinicians actually ask — what happens if we intervene — needs a causal framework, and a SHAP value is not one.
The model was never tested outside its own extract. Every figure today rests on 231 held-out rows from the same file as the 537 it was fitted on. Chapter 4 showed what happens when that assumption breaks; nothing since then has re-examined it.
The explanations themselves were never validated. We checked the arithmetic of SHAP and the control behaviour of the importance measures, but we never asked whether an explanation is stable across resamples of the training data. Refit the forest on a different split and the ranking below glucose rearranges itself. An explanation with no uncertainty attached is an estimate reported without a standard error.

Chapter 34 has the reading, and the module leaves you with the only durable habit on offer: before you explain a model, show that it is worth explaining.

title: 34  Roadmap — the rest of the module
text:
34.1 Principles the later days should keep
This booklet grows by teaching day. Six are written; the ones below that are not are the obvious continuations, each with the loose end it picks up. Appendix E explains how to add one.
Days 2 to 6 were built from the module’s earlier standalone sites, and the conversion changed three things on purpose: both languages now read the same file, every reported number is produced by code in the chapter rather than quoted from an earlier run, and each exercise carries a control. Each day’s dayN-CHANGES.md, kept out of the published booklet, records what differs from the original pages.
These are what make the booklet a course rather than a pile of notebooks.
crumbs: 34  Roadmap — the rest of the module

title: 34  Roadmap — the rest of the module
text:
Every exercise carries a control. A student who has only run a pipeline believes its output. One who has watched the same pipeline survive — or fail — a baseline, a shuffled label, or a no-shift extract believes the method. Day 1 has three controls: the predict-the-mean baseline, extract A, and the refitted-coefficient comparison.
Nothing is introduced before the object it acts on. Cross-validation is only meaningful once a student has felt a single split wobble.
Each exercise ends with what cannot be claimed. The limitation is not a disclaimer; it is the hook for the next day.
Both languages, every time. Where they genuinely differ, say so and say why, rather than presenting one as a translation of the other.
The provenance of every dataset is written down. Day 1’s data is simulated and its generating process is published, which is the only way a student can discover that their diagnosis was wrong. Days 2 to 6 use a synthetic diabetes dataset and two small clinical teaching files, documented in Appendix B — including why the dataset the exercises were originally written against is no longer used.
Every day fits on twenty printed pages. The site carries the discussion; the worksheet carries the tasks. If a day will not fit, the narrative moves into a ::: {.web-only} block rather than the tasks being cut.

title: Appendix A — Running it on your own machine
text:
A.2 Installation
install.packages(c("tidymodels", "tidyverse", "data.table", "rpart"))
You do not need conda. R can build and manage the Python environment for you, which is one less thing to install and one less thing to explain. From the project folder, in R:
source("scripts/setup_local.R")
That installs the R packages and then settles the Python side. You do not choose a Python, create an environment or activate anything: the project’s .Rprofile declares which libraries the {python} cells need, and reticulate assembles an environment to match the first time Python is used — downloading Python itself if your machine has none. The script just triggers that once, so the download does not land on you mid-exercise. Expect a few minutes the first time and nothing thereafter.






ImportantIf import pandas fails in a {python} cell



Your Python cells run through the reticulate bridge, and reticulate has found a Python that has no pandas — usually the one your operating system ships. Two things fix it, in this order: make sure you opened this project folder (so .Rprofile is read — getwd() should end in HDS_M3), and restart R. Then run source("scripts/setup_local.R"). If you have ever set RETICULATE_PYTHON yourself, in .Renviron or elsewhere, that overrides all of this; clear it.

A.5 Reproducibility habits to start now
Three things, each costing seconds, which save a day later in the module.

Set a seed before anything random, and say so in the text: set.seed(42) in R, random_state=42 in scikit-learn. Different values are fine; silence is not.
Record your environment at the end of any analysis you will show someone: sessionInfo() in R, pip freeze in Python.

title: Appendix B — The datasets
text:
B.1 los_data.csv — the training world
Day 1’s datasets are simulated by scripts/make_data.R, from seed 2025. Run Rscript scripts/make_data.R from the project root to regenerate all of them; data/PROVENANCE.txt records when and with which R version. Days 2 to 6 add three files that are not simulated here: a synthetic diabetes dataset shipped with mlbench, and two small clinical teaching files used in the preprocessing exercises. All five are described below.
Simulation is deliberate for Day 1, for three reasons. The generating process is known, so every diagnostic question has a checkable answer. No information governance approval is needed, so the files can live in a public repository. And the defects are the ones we chose, so they can be taught.
1000 admissions. Used in Exercises 1.2 and 1.3.
Known defects, retained on purpose.
Both of the first two are the subject of Exercise 1.2, Task 1.
These parameters match the los_data.csv distributed in earlier years of the module, so answers stated as ranges are unaffected by which copy a student has.

section: B.5 diabetes.csv — the case study for Days 2 to 6
text:
B.5 diabetes.csv — the case study for Days 2 to 6
768 adults, nine columns, exported from mlbench’s SynthDiabetes by scripts/make_data.R. Every value is synthetic and no row corresponds to a real person.







Column
Meaning




pregnant
number of times pregnant


glucose
plasma glucose concentration, glucose tolerance test


pressure
diastolic blood pressure, mm Hg


triceps
triceps skin fold thickness, mm


insulin
2-hour serum insulin, mu U/ml


mass
body mass index


pedigree
diabetes pedigree function


age
years


diabetes
pos or neg



Known defect, retained on purpose. Zeros appear where zero is physiologically impossible: 52.7% of insulin values, 32.7% of triceps, 4.6% of pressure, 1.7% of mass and 0.7% of glucose. They are missing values written as zeros, and because they are numerically valid, every summary statistic and every model will quietly use them. Finding them is the first task of Day 2, and they are what makes the imputation and leakage exercises bite.






ImportantWhy this is synthetic, and why that is worth five minutes of class



These exercises were originally written against PimaIndiansDiabetes: data on diabetes in Akimel O’odham (“Pima”) women, collected by the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, which reached the UCI Machine Learning Repository in the late 1980s and became one of the most-used teaching datasets in the world.
Both UCI and mlbench have since withdrawn it. The mlbench changelog for version 2.1-10 records the removal, and the documentation for the replacement states that the data “had apparently been included without informed consent” in those repositories, and that distribution ceased once it became clear the data “had most likely been shared illicitly”.
Copies remain on third-party mirrors, and nothing technical prevents their use. The reason this booklet does not use them is that a teaching repository is a publisher like any other. It is also a point worth making to the cohort directly: consent does not expire because a file is convenient, a dataset’s ubiquity is not evidence that it was lawfully obtained, and “everyone uses it” is the sentence that kept it in circulation for thirty years.
SynthDiabetes was created by Matthias Templ to mimic the data analysed by Smith et al. (1988). It has the same size, the same columns and the same defects, so the exercises are unchanged; only the values differ.

title: Appendix B — The datasets
text:
B.6 longisland_heart.csv — missingness to diagnose
200 patients, 14 columns, used in the Day 2 missing-data exercise. Each of the 13 predictors has exactly 20 missing values, and 150 of the 200 rows are incomplete in at least one column — a pattern regular enough that students can work out it was injected rather than observed, which is itself the point of the first task.
Two things to say out loud when you use it. The outcome, diagnosis of heart disease, has five levels rather than two. And the clinical variables are not in clinical units: trestbps runs from 1 to 41 and chol from 1 to 100, so they have been recoded or binned at some earlier point by someone who did not write it down. That is an ordinary and instructive state for a teaching extract to be in.

title: Appendix B — The datasets
section: B.7 bupa.csv — skewed variables to transform
text:
B.7 bupa.csv — skewed variables to transform
345 patients, seven columns of liver-related blood tests (mcv, alkalinephosphotase, alamine, aspartate, gammaGlut), plus drinks and a selector field. Complete, with no missing values. Used in the Day 2 transformation exercise because gammaGlut and alamine are strongly right-skewed, which is what makes a log transformation visibly do something.






NoteA caution worth passing on



selector is often treated as a disease label in tutorials using this file. It is not one: it was the field the original depositors used to split the data into two sets. It splits this copy 200 / 145, and mean daily drinks are 3.39 and 3.54 in the two groups — an arbitrary partition, not a diagnosis. Any exercise that predicts it is predicting the split. This booklet uses the file only for transformation, where the label is irrelevant: alamine, gammaGlut and aspartate have skewness 3.1, 2.9 and 2.3, which is what makes a log transformation visibly do something.

title: Appendix B — The datasets
text:
B.8 Using real data instead
Any of these can be swapped for a real dataset, and the booklet’s structure survives it, but two things change and should be said out loud when you do it. The known answer disappears, so the self-checks that compare against a key (check_shift_answers()) no longer apply; and the defects become the ones the extract happens to have rather than the ones the exercise needs. Teaching diagnosis first on data with a known answer, then on real data, is the order that works.

title: Appendix C — Troubleshooting
text:
C.3 Modelling

R: predict() returns 800 rows when the new data has 400

parsnip wants new_data =. With newdata = the argument is swallowed and you silently predict on the training data. The most expensive typo in the module.

Python: ValueError: Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead

X = df["Age"] gives a Series; scikit-learn wants a frame. Use df[["Age"]], with two sets of brackets.

The test MAE is suspiciously good (below 3 days)

You fitted on the full dataset rather than on train. Check the data = argument of fit().

The two languages give different numbers for the same model

Expected, if a random split is involved: set.seed(42) and random_state=42 select different rows. See the callout in Chapter 3. Not expected for coefficients, which should agree to several decimals.

C  Troubleshooting

title: Appendix C — Troubleshooting
text:
C.4 On your own machine

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas' in a {python} cell

reticulate has found a Python that is not the one this project declares. This is the most common local problem and has nothing to do with your code. Check three things, in order. (1) getwd() ends in HDS_M3 — if you opened a parent folder, the project’s .Rprofile was never read, and it is what declares the libraries. (2) Sys.getenv("RETICULATE_PYTHON") is empty — if you have set it, that Python is used as is and must have the libraries itself. (3) packageVersion("reticulate") is 1.41 or later; older versions cannot assemble an environment, so update and restart R. Then source("scripts/setup_local.R").

The Python console in Positron is labelled “Python (reticulate)”

That is the right one for {python} cells in a .qmd whose engine is knitr; R starts it and it is the bridge the chapters use. The separate “Python (System)” interpreter is not the one your cells run in, which is why installing packages into it does not help.

No such file or directory: 'data/los_data.csv' locally

Paths are relative to the project root. Open the .Rproj, or check getwd().

A column arrived as text

read_csv() prints what it guessed; read that message. The usual culprit is a sentinel such as "unknown" in a numeric column. Fix it in the col_types = argument, not by editing the file.

title: Appendix C — Troubleshooting
text:
C.5 Rendering the booklet

Rendering is slow

It executes every chapter the first time. After that freeze: auto replays the cached results, and only chapters you changed re-execute. Delete _freeze/ to force a full rebuild.

The printed worksheet is missing the tasks

scripts/make_worksheet.py builds it from the chapter sources. Re-run it after editing a chapter; the generated file in print/ is not meant to be edited.

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
Terms as this module uses them. Where a word has a different everyday meaning, that is noted, because the gap is where misunderstanding with clinical colleagues begins.

Baseline

A deliberately unintelligent predictor — here, the mean of the training outcome — against which a model’s error is compared. A model that does not beat its baseline has not been shown to have learnt anything.

Concept shift

A change in \(P(Y \mid X)\): the same patient would now have a different outcome. Undetectable without observed outcomes.

Covariate shift

A change in \(P(X)\) with \(P(Y \mid X)\) unchanged: different patients, same rules. Detectable from inputs alone. Not automatically harmful.

Feature

A predictor, a column of X. Clinicians say “variable” and mean the same thing.

Generalisation

Performance on data not used to fit the model. In this module it always means something you measured, never something you hope for.

Held-out / test set

Rows withheld from fitting and used once, at the end, to estimate generalisation. Used twice, it stops being a test set.

Leakage

Any route by which information about the outcome, or about the test rows, reaches the model during fitting. Produces scores that are too good and cannot be reproduced.

MAE — mean absolute error

The average absolute difference between prediction and truth, in the outcome’s own units. Treats all errors in proportion to their size.

Pipeline

The ordered sequence load → define X and y → split → fit → evaluate. The order is the content: the split must precede the fit, and the evaluation must follow it.

Prediction vs inference

Prediction asks how close \(\hat{y}\) is to \(y\). Inference asks whether a relationship is real and how large it is. The same linear model serves both, which is why the same lm() call appears in Module 2 and this one with different purposes.

Training set

The rows the model is allowed to see while its parameters are estimated.

Residual

Observed minus predicted, for one row. Averaging their absolute values gives MAE; plotting them against the prediction shows whose predictions are bad.

E.1 1. Scaffold it
A new teaching day is five files and a block of configuration. This chapter is the procedure.

That writes day2-00-overview.qmd, one chapter per exercise named, and day2-99-consolidation.qmd from _templates/exercise.qmd, and registers the part: block in _quarto.yml. Re-running it leaves existing files alone, so it is safe to use again when you add a fourth exercise to a day.

E.2 2. Check it before you publish
make check
scripts/check_cells.py catches the faults that render cleanly and then fail in front of a student: a task chunk missing eval: false, a worked answer outside the when-meta="show-solutions" block (which would publish it before the session), and a link to a chapter that does not exist. E.3 3. Add any new data to the generator
Append to scripts/make_data.R; do not write a second script. One generator with one seed is what makes every student’s copy identical and every expected value quotable. New data files are published automatically, since project: resources: includes data/.

section: E.4 4. Add a check, if the exercise needs one
text:
E.4 4. Add a check, if the exercise needs one
checks/checks.R and checks/checks.py are deliberately small. A new check wraps hds_check():
check_folds <- function(folds, n_expected = 5) {
  hds_check(paste0("there are ", n_expected, " folds"),
            nrow(folds) == n_expected,
            hint = "check the v = argument of vfold_cv()",
            detail = paste(nrow(folds), "folds"))
}
Write the Python twin at the same time. A check that exists in one language only quietly turns the booklet into a single-language course.

text:
E.6 Writing the cells







You want
How




a worked example, shown with its output
a plain ```{r} or ```{python} chunk


a task for the student to fill in
the same, plus #\| eval: false, with ______ where the answer goes


a hint
a ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} block — name the function, never the line


the worked answer
a ::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"} block containing an executed chunk



Two rules, each learnt the hard way.

A task chunk must be eval: false. ______ is not valid code, so the render fails without it. make check catches it.
Hints are always visible. A hint containing the answer line publishes the answer; name the functions instead.

text:
E.7 Keeping the worksheet under twenty pages
scripts/make_worksheet.py drops solutions, hints, instructor blocks and web-only notes, and flattens the R/Python tabs into labels, which is most of the saving. Day 1 comes out at 14 pages for students and 16 for staff. If a day runs long, the thing to cut is narrative, not tasks: move the discussion into a ::: {.web-only} block, where it stays on the site and leaves the paper.

title: Appendix E — Adding a day
text:
E.9 Two conventions worth keeping
Solutions go in solution: true cells and instructor commentary in content-visible when-profile="instructor", never in a collapsed callout. A collapsed callout still ships the text inside the student HTML, two clicks away in the page source.
Quote expected values as ranges. make_data.R is reproducible, but anyone who changes an n or adds a draw shifts the random stream downstream. “MAE ≈ 3.2–3.4 days” survives that; “MAE = 3.423” does not.
